title: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition) · Units 47–48
description: Source-reviewed upper-intermediate language for bodily actions, facial expressions, praise, criticism, evaluations and idioms.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-provided book for personal study. Vocabulary selection and distinctions follow the source units; examples and explanatory notes are newly written. Original textbook passages, exercises and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Teaching pages for Units 47–48, captions, illustrations, language help, exercises 47.1–47.5 and 48.1–48.5, and corresponding answer-key entries reviewed for vocabulary coverage and usage.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA for checked straightforward words; longer idioms omit IPA rather than supply uncertain connected-speech transcriptions. Some expressions use a short speechText to support natural word audio.
audit.languagePolicy: All content is English except natural Brazilian Portuguese translations in pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Manual review of the exact source teaching, image and exercise pages and answer key; lexical and contextual checks, original example drafting, structural and audio-field validation. No live VocabLab or browser audio testing was done.
audit.limitations: No bundled recordings. Live import, TTS voice quality and speech recognition have not been tested.

units.title: Unit 47 — What your body does
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 100–101 (PDF pages 101–102).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Recognise and use precise verbs for breathing, eating, eye movements, facial expressions and whole-body actions.
Distinguish nearby meanings such as blink versus wink, shiver versus tremble, and chew versus swallow.
Use recurring collocations, prepositions and forms such as sigh with relief, grin from ear to ear and shake with laughter.
Distinguish breathe from breath, sweat from perspire, and regular verbs from irregular bite and shake.

sectionsChecked: A: Verbs connected with the mouth and breathing
C: Verbs connected with the eyes and face
D: Verbs connected with the whole body
Language help: irregular verbs and corresponding nouns

items.example: I started to yawn during the late-night presentation.
items.note: To open your mouth widely when tired or bored; also a noun.

items.example: The dusty cupboard made her sneeze repeatedly.
items.note: A sudden burst of air through the nose and mouth; also a noun.

items.example: My brother sometimes snores so loudly that I cannot sleep.
items.note: To make a noisy breathing sound while asleep.

items.example: The smoke made everyone cough.
items.note: To force air suddenly from your throat; the noun has the same spelling.

items.example: He sighed when he realised how much work was left.
items.note: To breathe out audibly, often expressing disappointment, tiredness or relief.

items.example: We sighed with relief when the missing dog came home.
items.note: A common collocation describing relief after worry.

items.example: I was out of breath after climbing six flights of stairs.
items.note: Describes difficulty breathing normally after exertion; not the same as holding your breath.

items.example: Take a deep breath before you begin your speech.
items.note: To draw a large amount of air into your lungs.

items.example: The swimmer held her breath while she passed under the bridge.
items.note: To stop breathing briefly, deliberately; hold becomes held in the past.

items.example: It is easier to breathe once the room has fresh air.
items.note: The verb ends in a voiced /ð/ sound; contrast the noun breath /breθ/.

items.example: His breath was visible in the cold morning air.
items.note: The noun has a final /θ/ sound, unlike the verb breathe /briːð/.

items.example: Chew your food carefully before swallowing it.
items.note: To crush food with your teeth; contrast with swallow.

items.example: Her stomach began to rumble during the quiet exam.
items.note: A stomach can rumble when you are hungry; also used for low continuous noises.

items.example: She swallowed the tablet with a glass of water.
items.note: To move food, drink or medicine from your mouth to your stomach.

items.example: The toddler sucked through a straw to finish the juice.
items.note: To draw liquid or air into the mouth; one common pattern is suck through a straw.

items.example: The child licked the ice cream before it melted.
items.note: To move your tongue over something, especially food.

items.example: Be careful not to bite your tongue while eating.
items.note: Irregular verb: bite, bit, bitten; chewing involves repeated bites.

items.pt: bocado; porção que cabe na boca
items.example: He took one mouthful of soup and then asked for more.
items.note: A quantity of food or drink held in the mouth; plural mouthfuls.

items.pt: piscar um olho; dar uma piscadela
items.example: My colleague winked at me to show that he was joking.
items.note: To close and open one eye deliberately; wink at someone.

items.example: She frowned when she saw the unexpected test result.
items.note: To draw your eyebrows together, usually because you are worried or displeased.

items.example: He grinned when he heard that his team had won.
items.note: A broad smile, often expressing pleasure or amusement.

items.example: She was grinning from ear to ear after passing her driving test.
items.note: An idiom describing a very broad, happy smile.

items.example: I blinked several times after walking into the bright sunlight.
items.note: To shut and open both eyes quickly; unlike wink, it is generally not deliberate communication.

items.example: He blushed when everybody applauded his speech.
items.note: To turn red in the face because of embarrassment or strong emotion.

items.example: I always sweat during an intense workout.
items.note: Everyday word for producing moisture through the skin; can also be a noun.

items.example: Some people perspire heavily when they feel nervous.
items.note: More formal than sweat; noun: perspiration.

items.example: Perspiration appeared on his forehead in the warm room.
items.note: Noun corresponding to perspire; do not use perspire as a noun.

items.example: The children shivered while waiting in the cold rain.
items.note: Small involuntary movements, especially from cold or fear.

items.example: Her hands trembled as she opened the important letter.
items.note: To shake slightly, especially from fear, nerves or weakness.

items.example: The windows shook as the heavy lorry passed.
items.note: Irregular verb: shake, shook, shaken; can involve a stronger movement than tremble.

items.example: We were shaking with laughter by the end of his story.
items.note: Exercise-checked expression for movements caused by intense laughter.

items.example: The frightened puppy was trembling with fear.
items.note: Exercise-checked verb-preposition combination showing the cause of trembling.

units.title: Unit 48 — Praising and criticising
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 102–103 (PDF pages 103–104).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Use expressions for praising abilities, outstanding performance and quality, including British informal idioms.
Distinguish criticism as disapproval from critical evaluation and recognise the four meanings of critical.
Use idiomatic negative evaluations accurately, including take the biscuit, pick holes in and have your cake and eat it.
Choose accurate collocations and grammatical patterns for both praise and criticism, including praise for and critical of.

sectionsChecked: A: Praising, skill and positive idioms
B: Criticising, meanings of critical and critically, and negative idioms

items.example: The supervisor praised the trainees for their careful work.
items.note: Pattern: praise someone for something; can be a verb or noun.

items.example: The research paper was highly praised by the reviewers.
items.note: Common collocation; highly intensifies praise, rather than meaning physically high.

items.example: She explained the difficult concept brilliantly.
items.note: Adverb describing something done with exceptional skill.

items.example: The laboratory provides first-rate technical support.
items.note: Strongly positive evaluation; the hyphenated adjective usually precedes a noun.

items.example: They hired a top-notch technician for the project.
items.note: Informal approving adjective for exceptionally good quality.

items.pt: de terceira categoria; de má qualidade
items.example: The hotel advertised luxury but offered third-rate service.
items.note: Negative contrast with first-rate; appears in the opposite-meaning exercise.

items.example: The new engineer is on the ball and spots problems quickly.
items.note: Informal idiom for alertness and quick understanding.

items.example: Our teacher has a way with nervous students.
items.note: Means being especially good at communicating with or managing people or animals.

items.example: My neighbour has green fingers and grows beautiful roses.
items.note: British idiom meaning to be good at gardening; American equivalent: have a green thumb.

items.word: have the gift of the gab
items.pt: ter muita lábia; falar com desenvoltura
items.example: She has the gift of the gab and enjoys hosting public events.
items.note: Informal expression for fluent, persuasive or engaging speech.

items.pt: muito superior a; bem acima de
items.example: The lead researcher was head and shoulders above the other candidates.
items.note: Especially common in comparisons of people or their abilities.

items.example: The revised design is miles better than the first one.
items.note: Informal intensifier for a large difference in quality; often followed by than.

items.example: This new tool is streets ahead of the older version.
items.note: Often streets ahead of someone or something in quality or progress.

items.example: The new research facility is among the best in the country.
items.note: Among marks membership of a high-performing group, rather than one single winner.

items.example: That was among the worst customer experiences I have had.
items.note: Negative counterpart of among the best, included as a contrast in the teaching section.

items.example: The dessert at that restaurant was out of this world.
items.note: Informal, enthusiastic praise, especially for food or other experiences.

items.pt: quando se trata de; no que diz respeito a
items.example: When it comes to testing, she is exceptionally thorough.
items.note: Introduces the subject on which a judgement is based.

items.word: as far as something is concerned
items.pt: no que diz respeito a algo
items.example: As far as safety is concerned, the checks must be repeated.
items.note: Formal topic-framing expression; word audio uses a short naturally spoken instance.
items.speechText: as far as safety is concerned

items.example: The manager criticised the team's poor record-keeping.
items.note: One sense: to express disapproval; British spelling criticise.

items.example: Students were asked to criticise two short films in their essays.
items.note: Another sense: to evaluate a work, including both strengths and weaknesses.

items.pt: crítico em relação a; contrário a
items.example: The inspection report was critical of the outdated procedures.
items.note: Means expressing disapproval; usually critical of someone or something.

items.example: Reliable measurements are critical to the success of the trial.
items.note: Here critical means extremely important, not negative.

items.example: Her critical appraisal considered both the book's strengths and its flaws.
items.note: An informed evaluation of a text, performance or other work.

items.pt: aclamação da crítica; elogio dos críticos
items.example: The director's latest film received critical acclaim.
items.note: Recognition or praise from professional reviewers and critics.

items.example: Accurate calibration is critically important for these measurements.
items.note: Intensifier based on the importance sense of critical.

items.example: The critically acclaimed play sold out within days.
items.note: The adjective refers to strong approval from reviewers, not to a dangerous condition.

items.example: The patient remained critically ill throughout the night.
items.note: Very seriously ill; another meaning of critically.

items.example: The injured cyclist was taken to hospital in a critical condition.
items.note: Indicates a dangerous medical state; contrast with critical of, meaning disapproving.

items.example: He kept running down his colleagues during the meeting.
items.note: Informal phrasal verb meaning to criticise unfairly or negatively in this context.

items.pt: procurar defeitos em; ficar apontando falhas
items.example: It is easy to pick holes in someone else's proposal.
items.note: Informal idiom: search for weaknesses, often excessively.

items.example: The suggestion that we could finish in one hour was absurd.
items.note: A strong negative judgement: completely unreasonable or ridiculous.

items.example: The operator was not at fault for the damaged cable.
items.note: Indicates responsibility for a mistake or problem; often with be.

items.example: Neither student was to blame for the equipment failure.
items.note: Means responsible for something bad; typically be to blame for.

items.pt: o máximo; alguém que se acha excelente
items.example: He thinks he is the cat's whiskers just because he won once.
items.note: Informal ironic idiom: used about a person who thinks they are wonderful.

items.example: She acts as though her new phone is the bee's knees.
items.note: Informal expression for something considered excellent, sometimes ironic.

items.example: I must be the world's worst person at remembering birthdays.
items.note: Emphatic or humorous negative superlative.

items.pt: passar dos limites; ser o cúmulo
items.example: Charging extra for a broken chair really takes the biscuit.
items.note: British informal idiom: an especially striking or annoying bad example.

items.word: have your cake and eat it
items.pt: querer ter tudo sem abrir mão de nada
items.example: You cannot take the promotion and keep the same free time; you cannot have your cake and eat it.
items.note: To want two attractive but incompatible advantages.

items.example: Two passengers were critically injured in the collision.
items.note: Exercise-linked use of critically: an injury is life-threatening or very serious.
